module_title: Computer Architecture - ISA, Pipelining, and Advanced Topologies
introduction: Tailored for IT Specialist Officers (Bank SO), SSC CGL Tier-2, and advanced technical operators, this module analyzes complex CPU design methodologies, the critical differences between RISC and CISC instruction sets, and advanced execution overlapping techniques.

core_concepts.title: Von Neumann Architecture
core_concepts.description: The standard architecture used in most general-purpose computers. Its defining feature is a 'Unified Memory'—meaning both Data and Instructions share the exact same memory space and travel across the same physical data bus.

core_concepts.title: Harvard Architecture
core_concepts.description: An alternative design where Data and Instructions are stored in completely separate, physically distinct memory units with separate buses. This allows the CPU to fetch data and instructions simultaneously. Widely used in Microcontrollers and DSPs.

core_concepts.title: Instruction Set Architecture (RISC vs. CISC)
core_concepts.description:
- RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer): Utilizes simple, highly optimized instructions that mostly execute in a single clock cycle (e.g., ARM processors, Apple Silicon). Emphasizes software.
- CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer): Utilizes complex, multi-step instructions that take several clock cycles to execute (e.g., Intel x86). Emphasizes hardware.

core_concepts.title: Pipelining
core_concepts.description: An advanced CPU throughput technique where multiple instructions are overlapped during execution. While instruction 'A' is being Executed, instruction 'B' is being Decoded, and instruction 'C' is being Fetched simultaneously, drastically improving overall processor efficiency.

important_entities.name: Multi-core Processing
important_entities.key_fact: Multiple CPUs on a Single Die
important_entities.significance: A dual-core or quad-core processor contains two or four independent physical processing units (ALU+CU) on a single chip, allowing true parallel execution of tasks.

important_entities.name: Cache Memory Hierarchy
important_entities.significance: L1 is the smallest and fastest cache built directly into the core. L2 is slightly larger and slower. L3 is the largest cache, generally shared across all the cores on a multi-core chip to sync data.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Because Von Neumann architecture forces data and instructions to share a single bus, the CPU (which is lightning fast) often sits idle waiting for memory (which is slower) to deliver data. This idle waiting period is universally termed the 'Von Neumann Bottleneck'.

In statement-based Tier-2 questions, remember that RISC architecture uses a strict 'Load/Store' architecture (memory can only be accessed by specific load/store commands, not by math operations directly). CISC allows math operations directly on memory.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Harvard gives you two separate degrees
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Link the elite name 'Harvard' with the premium architecture that uses TWO physically separate memory units and buses (one for Data, one for Instructions).

exam_strategy_tips: In highly analytical exams, examiners will test your understanding of Cache Hierarchy. Remember the proximity rule: L1 is closest to the core (fastest/smallest), while L3 is furthest (slowest/largest shared pool).
